title: The Play That Drained a City
story:
By the time the company of actors reached the lands of the demons, their fame ran ahead of them. Everywhere they performed, the Asuras rose from their seats, delighted, and pressed jewels into their hands; in the city of Supura the citizens were so enchanted they begged for more. What the demons never guessed was that the troupe's newest players were not actors at all. They were Pradyumna, Gada, Shamba and the other Yadava heroes in the costumes of the stage, led by Bhadra — the actor who had been granted the boon to wander freely through all the three worlds.

The city of Vajra was supposed to be impossible to enter. Even the wind could not pass its walls unless the demon king Vajranabha willed it. But kings have appetites, and when Vajranabha heard of the marvellous actors he did what any patron of the arts would do: he sent a messenger, and invited them in. The demons of the branch cities brought the troupe to the charming city of Vajra, lodged them in a house built by the celestial architect, and supplied everything they could need by the hundred.

Vajranabha raised a beautiful pavilion and made a festival of the visit. The women of his family watched from behind a screen where they could see everything; the king himself sat among his kinsmen. And the actors began.

First the instruments — bells, flutes, drums — and then the women of the troupe sang the celestial song Chhalikya, the very music the Yadavas had brought down from heaven. They sang of the descent of the Ganga in seven scales and three modes, in the raga Vasanta and its kin, so sweetly that the Asuras rose again and again to heap rewards on them. Then came the Ramayana itself: the birth of Vishnu for the destruction of Ravana, and how the sage Rishyashringa was brought to King Dasharatha. The demons were startled by the likeness of the players — it seemed impossible that actors should resemble Rama and Lakshmana and Bharata so closely — and they rose from their seats, called out their praise, and gave away necklaces of gold and vaidurya, bracelets and cloth.

After the Ramayana, Pradyumna himself, still in the guise of an actor, conducted the prologue with Gada and Shamba, and Rukmini's son sang the hymn of the descent of the Ganga with beautiful gestures. Then came the drama Rambhabhisara: Shura played Ravana, Monovati played Rambha, Pradyumna played Nalakuvara and Shamba his jester. By their illusory powers the Yadavas conjured the very scene of Kailasha, and acted how the furious Nalakuvara cursed the wicked Ravana, and how Rambha was consoled.

The Danavas were enchanted. Costly garments, jewelled necklaces, sky-going chariots and celestial elephants, cool sandal and aguru and rare scents, and at last the fabled gem Chintamani, which grants whatever its owner thinks of — all of it rained upon the actors, scene after scene, until the treasuries of the demon lords ran dry. Even the women of the Danava chiefs gave away their jewels. The demons were deprived of their riches, the text says, precisely in the act of trying to spend them.

Only slowly did they understand. They had paid their enemies to entertain them — and the Yadavas, welcomed through gates that no army could ever have breached, had walked into the unbreachable city of Vajra.

Behind the screen, where the women of the Asura's own family sat watching, Vajranabha's daughter Prabhavati had received a message carried from Dwaraka. Her friend Suchimukhi whispered that she had seen Pradyumna himself, and that he had appointed this very evening to meet her. The Bhaimas never speak untruth — and so, the goose assured her, that night she would see her love.
reflection: The city that no army could enter was entered by applause: the demons paid their enemies to entertain them and never suspected that the pleasure they bought was their own ruin. There is something almost courteous in the way the Yadavas take Vajra — not by storm, but by invitation.
next_story_tease: The emptied treasuries were only the beginning, for Vajranabha had already set his heart on conquering heaven.
hero_scene: Inside the pavilion of Vajra, Pradyumna in actor's costume performs the role of Nalakuvara upon a stage that, by illusion, shows the very summit of Kailasha, while the Danava lords rise around him to shower gold, gems and sky-chariots upon the players.
